note: The configuration this project measured as best, as data, because it was living in three places at once — a Python constant, a workflow input, and a reader's memory of the last round — and a product that ships a different placement from the one the number was measured at is a product whose number does not apply to it. `packages/core/src/memory/serving.ts` exports this file's values as `SERVING_DEFAULTS`, and a test in each repository reads the file: change `placement` here and exactly one test fails on each side, which is the only version of 'the product uses the measured configuration' that a build can check.
confirmedBy: R216b (run 45630594988, 2026-11-25): front 93/114 (81.6%) against board 96/114 (84.2%), +2.6 pp [-7.2, +12.5], McNemar p = 0.6776; bill per episode $0.00583 against $0.00558 (-4%); attribution 65.7% of writing episodes. The placement is confirmed: it is cheaper and it does not cost accuracy.

placement.evidence: a block in the system message re-bills every token after it, and R216b measured the price at the same 114 tasks and seed: $0.00583 an episode in front against $0.00558 behind the conversation (-4%), with the accuracy contrast +2.6 pp [-7.2, +12.5] - no movement the grid can resolve, which is the outcome a placement should have. The -4% is smaller than R216-1's +37% front-versus-control gap implies because the block only moved on 23% of turns: the prefix is re-bought on a change, not on a turn.

askSource.evidence: asks taken from the request rather than every tool result took the list from 10.6 a turn to 1.96, and moved the arm from -5.3 pp to +4.4 pp. R228, R229 and R230 have since priced the three alternatives and none replaced it: binding the item to the record the episode read covers 98.5% at 2.53 unneeded open items an episode (R228, refused on the open tax), binding an ask to that record covers 415 of 654 against the request board's 416 (R229, refused on settlement), and admitting a later turn only where the assistant had not asked a question recovers 25 of 155 later-turn writes and covers 62.7%, below the contract (R230, refused on recovery and coverage). The request is the only ask source either repository has measured that pays, which is why this value has not moved in four rounds. R231 has since measured the one alternative that beats the request board on accuracy and refused it on price: clause admission covers 95.4% of the required writes for 17.72 items per rescued write, so `request` remains the only ask source that is both measured and affordable, and the round's actionable consequence is a parser scope (no inheritance across a turn boundary) rather than a second source. R232 has since changed what the efficiency refusal means without changing the value: measured at the moment of each graded write, the clause board is 8.10 items a call and displays an open ask for 622 of the 654 required writes (95.1%, 14 hidden of 636 reached), so the 17.72 items per rescued write belongs to the finished board and the rendered cost is bounded by the cap at eight lines. What keeps `request` here is no longer price but evidence: no dispatch has measured clause admission's effect on task success.

settlementGrades.evidence: a name-only grade settled 2 of 107 episodes for a set-shaped ask; the overlap grade (at least one shared content word and half the shorter side) is what made attribution 75.5%. `loose` is counted rather than assumed away.

blockCeilingChars.evidence: asserted in the mechanism gate: a block above 500 characters is a list of everything rather than a contract.

openAskCeiling.evidence: asserted in the mechanism gate. Above three open asks a turn the block stops being a contract and becomes a transcript.

notYet.admissionPolicy: R219 — the invocation policy, read twice. The rule admits the block's state lines and refuses its two judgment lines, which name a family the task requires a write in on 1,808 of 1,965 entries (92.0%) over R218b's 456 episodes. Two identical dispatches read +10.5 pp (p = 0.029) and -0.9 pp (p = 1.0); pooled +4.8 pp [-1.2, +10.8], p = 0.152. The mechanism replicated exactly both times (admission all/state, 8% shorter block, 19% fewer changes, 4% and 7% cheaper), so the null is about the effect and not about the treatment. NOT promoted: a product default is a measured configuration, and this measurement returns no effect at 114 tasks. It stays a correctness repair with a measured cost saving; R222 prices the 1,600-episode reading that could support an accuracy claim.
notYet.servingDecision: R223 - the serving decision, screened and refused on artefacts already on disk. 385 prefix cuts over R218b's 228 paired episodes yielded one admissible policy, which did not replicate on the held-out half (+13.8 pp at p = 0.0074 on the screen half, +3.2 pp at p = 0.66 on the confirm half); at that many cuts noise alone yields about 9.6, so the family carries no signal. No default moves, and that is the round's product consequence: the shipped configuration is unchanged because nothing was promoted. What the round licenses is the next proxy - the material would have to be served from what the episode reveals after the identity gate, because every observable available before that point is constant within a task on 100% of tasks. Correction, R225 (AUDIT 34.315): the closing clause was wrong as written. The prefix is NOT constant within a task on 100% of tasks - the user simulator paraphrases, so the opening turn's length varies inside a task on 100% of tasks and the first tool call on 4% - and the correct statement is the weaker one the reading actually needs: no prefix observable that a request declares separates the pairs, at 96% task-constancy for the categorical fields and 20% for the ask count.
notYet.dose: R218e - the amount of material an episode receives, measured with the task held fixed and read at two scales. Whole grid: 28 discordant tasks, 14 for the higher dose and 14 against, 86 level, p = 1.0000, with the higher-dose side running 7 turns longer on the median task so the reading carries the length confound. Length-matched within one turn: 17 tasks, 2 against 3, 12 level, 5 discordant, p = 1.0000 - five is under the six a unanimous sign test needs, so that scale is a bound and not a verdict. No default moves: the block's size has no measurable effect on whether an episode passes, which closes the third of the three levers on improving memory (more material, better material, conditional material) and leaves only whether to serve at all.
notYet.revealedServingDecision: R225 - the successor R223 named, screened for nothing. The prefix now ends at the reveal's own result - the payload of the first call outside the authentication gate, which is the state R219's invocation policy has in hand when it serves - and six structural quantities are read from it: shape, length, keys, entries, leaves and variant axes. 565 cuts over R218b's 456 pairs yield 18 admissible against 14.1 from noise alone (z = +1.04, p = 0.148), and the cut the screen chose (skip records with 52 leaves or more) reverses sign on the half it never saw: -6.5 pp on 17 discordant pairs, 6 up and 11 down, p = 0.3323. The reveal is nearly as task-constant as the request (89-93% for the structural fields), so a cut on it is an admission rule for a task class too. No default moves, and this is the fourth consecutive round whose product consequence is that the shipped configuration is correct. What the two screens together establish is the thing the lane can now say: the harm is a property of the material's PRESENCE, not of its content (R218b, 8.98, 8.99), its amount (R218e) or its timing (R223, R225).
notYet.turnAdmission: R230 - the third ask source, considered and refused, so no knob is added. The rule admits a later-turn ask only when the assistant's previous turn did not ask a question, which needs no vocabulary and is the strongest structural filter available; it recovers 25 of the 155 writes R229 attributed to later turns (16.1%) and covers 410 of 654 required writes, BELOW the request board's 416, while opening 1,110 items. The mechanism is a property of the corpus's user model rather than of the rule: 1,893 of 2,453 user turns (77.2%) follow an assistant question, so a turn is both the answer and the requirement - and 52 episodes read their contract from a turn that is not turn one (`request_of` falls back to the first turn that states an ask), which the filter refused in 50 of them. That is how a board that reads MORE turns covers fewer writes, and it is the sharpest argument in this file for not shipping a second ask source: the shipped one is the contract, and the contract is read from the turn that states it. R231 restricts inheritance to the contract's turn instead of gating whole turns; it is registered and unread.
notYet.clauseAdmission: R231 - clause admission, the fourth ask source, considered and **not** shipped as a default although it is the first rule in this lane to reach the accuracy target. It reads the contract's turn whole and, from every later turn, only the clauses that name their own family; on R218b's 456 episodes it recovers 154 of the 155 later-turn writes (99.4%) and covers 624 of 654 required writes (95.4%, against the request board's 63.6%). It is refused on its efficiency bar: 2,729 items over the contract for those 154 writes, 17.72 each against a budget of 1.5. The refusal is not a defect of the rule but a property of the corpus - 5,311 asks offered across 2,453 user turns for 654 required writes, 8.1 per required write - so no admission rule that reads turns can price a rescue at 1.5 items. What it does establish is where the requirement lives, and that inheritance is the noise (dropping 1,153 inheritance-reached asks costs exactly one covered write): a future product change should restrict family inheritance to the turn that states the contract, which is a parser scope change and not a second ask source. R232 has since measured the display and found the price objection is to an artefact that is never rendered: at the moment of a call the clause board holds 8.10 items and shows 622 of the 654 required writes (95.1%) with 14 hidden, so its efficiency deficit is a property of the finished board and the cap bounds it at eight lines. The rule is therefore shippable on price and visibility and unmeasured on accuracy, which is the dispatch R234 prices and the reason this key still says not shipped.
notYet.displayOrder: R232/R233 - the rendering, measured for the first time. R232 took the board the product would serve at the moment of every graded write and asked whether an open ask of that write's family was among the eight lines: the clause board reaches 636 of 654 (97.2%), shows 622 (95.1%) and hides 14 (2.2%); the contract board reaches and shows 463 (70.8%) at 2.41 items a call. Two consequences, neither of which moves a default on its own. First, the block's size is a property of the moment and not of the episode - 8.10 items against 3,699 at the end - so any rule priced on the finished board has been priced on an object no agent ever sees, and R231's 17.72 items a rescued write should be read with that correction. Second, the fourteen hidden writes are an ordering fact: the block lists asks in statement order, so a settled ask outranks an open one stated later, and the case inspected by hand needed line nine. R233 registers `open before settled, statement order within each group` before its own reading; nothing is promoted until it is read, and even then the rendered block is not the agent's behaviour, which is what R234 would have to buy. R233 has since tested the first ordering and it is the first rendering change in this lane that a product could adopt on its own terms: `open before settled, statement order inside each group` is a stable partition of a list the board has already built, it lifts the clause board from 622 to 632 of 654 shown (95.1% to 96.6%), removes ten of the fourteen hidden writes (2.2% to 0.6%), loses none, and leaves the contract at 463 against its own 463. It is refused on its own bar by three writes, and the four that remain are hidden by repetition - a `modify` ask behind nine to thirty-nine open asks of one or two families, in a block 41 items long that holds nine `address` asks - so the next rendering rule is a fold (`one line per family`, R234), not a larger cap. Nothing is promoted: the ordering is measured on a deterministic board and not on a model's behaviour, and the dispatch that would join the two is the clause rule's accuracy run at ¥34.

carrier.why: The arm whose `--note-source` is the manifest's placement. Without this name the check is satisfied by any arm that happens to serve the same placement, so changing `placement` in the manifest would leave both readers green while the dispatch kept the old one. With it, changing `placement` fails the Python reader too, because `board` still carries the old placement.
